opennyai_summary.facts:
After following the procedure,
complaint was filed for violation of sections 2(ix)(k) and 7(ii) of the PFA Act and Rule 32 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules (hereinafter referred to as the "PFA Rules").
4.
opennyai_summary.arguments:
5. Learned counsel for the respondent submitted that of printing was not clear and, therefore, the information/entry made in the label was the subject matter of prosecution.
As per requirement of rt the PFA Rules the date of packaging was necessary and important, for ou without the date of packaging it is not possible to make out the expiry C date of the product.
Therefore, it is misbranding.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
So far as the right of h the petitioner for sending second sample for analysis to the Laboratory ig is concerned, that right is only available when adulteration is found.
H Section 13(2)
of the PFA Act, if read in its proper perspective, shows that second sample can be sent for analysis only when food article is adulterated or of sub-standard.
Hence, it is not a case, in which, the provision of section 13(2) of PFA Act is attracted and there is no violation of the rights of the accused.
When there is no mention of date of packaging, therefore, sample is misbranded under section 2(ix)(k) of PFA Act read with Rule 32 of PFA Rules.
Thus, this Analyst Report dated 04.11.2010 does not disclose that it is sub-standard or adulterated.
The charge has not been adulterated.
Charge has not been framed for sub-standard or adulteration of food article.
Secondly, the provision of section 13(2) of PFA Act for sending the second sample for analysis is not required as it is not a case of adulteration.
If the batch Hindustan Cocacola Beverages vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 6 March, 2018 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/134028399/
2 number and the manufacturing date were stated C on the wrapper of the food articles, it was sufficient compliance of the h Rules framed under the Act.
When this date of packaging or manufacturing is not made clear, it would be very difficult for the consumer to find out when the bottle was packed or manufactured.
Hence, not disclosing the date of package, definitely falls in the category of "misbranding".
Misbranding has been defined under sub-section (m)(ix) of section 2 of the PFA Act, in which, if it is not labelled in accordance with the Act or the Rules, it can be termed as "misbranded".
